name: LEO I business computer
summary: LEO I, built by the Lyons catering firm on the model of Cambridge's EDSAC, ran a bakery costing job in 1951, an early computer doing routine office work.
description: The J. Lyons & Company LEO I electronic stored-program computer, including development informed by EDSAC and its later Bakery Valuations office work.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.
why: Lyons ran a large catering business with heavy clerical work and wanted to automate its office calculations.

date.basis: Evidence for this dated community entry; not necessarily the first possible use.

events.statement: LEO I ran a bakery costing job for its company.
events.scope: LEO I computer running the Bakery Valuations office calculation at J. Lyons & Company.
events.caveats: Later full business dependence began separately; do not claim the computer was offered to outside buyers in 1951.

evidence.supports: LEO I ran a bakery costing job for its company.

contributions.resource: Used LEO I for a bakery costing job.

evidence.supports: The museum connects LEO I and its bakery valuation job to J. Lyons & Company.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. Evidence for this dated community entry; not necessarily the first possible use. Later full business dependence began separately; do not claim the computer was offered to outside buyers in 1951. This is the earliest supported record currently established here, not certification of absolute priority.

community_entry.rationale: A real internal business job is stronger than a prototype test; internal use need not be a commercial sale.
community_entry.caveats: Later full business dependence began separately; do not claim the computer was offered to outside buyers in 1951.

caveats: The 1951 bakery job remains a specific use of the computer. Later full business dependence began separately; no outside commercial computer offer is asserted for 1951.

links.statement: Lyons drew on the EDSAC project experience to develop LEO I.
links.scope: Cambridge and Lyons collaboration; hardware and design programme, not the later 1950 formal service as a causal prerequisite.
links.alternatives: Other computer designs and business requirements also influenced LEO.
links.caveats: The knowledge exchange began in 1947 before the 1950 program-service anchor.
links.timing: The July 1947 exchange of EDSAC experience precedes the 1951 LEO job; it is distinct from EDSAC’s 1950 formal service.

evidence.locator: LEO paragraph, July 1947 Lyons agreement and EDSAC experience
evidence.supports: The Cambridge history states that Lyons acquired EDSAC experience and LEO I was derived from EDSAC.

research.note: Proposed distinct configuration and community entry; requires independent review.
